draft.title: Corporate social responsibility
card: Corporate social responsibility (CSR) means a business acts for the good of workers, communities and the environment. It does this beyond what the law requires.
Obeying the law is the minimum. A business that only does what the law demands is not showing CSR.
Examples include cutting waste, using less energy, paying for staff training or flexible hours, and supporting a local community.
CSR is a choice the business makes. It can cost money in the short term, and a business may also gain a better reputation from it.
draft.remember: CSR is a business choosing to do good for workers, communities and the environment beyond its legal duties.

a.q: A bakery wants to show corporate social responsibility. Which action fits?
opts: A bakery chooses to donate unsold bread to a local shelter
A bakery pays its staff the award wage the law sets
A bakery follows food safety rules so it can open
A bakery lowers its prices to attract more customers
a.why: Donating unsold bread is a voluntary act that helps the community and goes beyond the law. Paying the award wage is tempting, but the law requires it, so it is only the minimum.
a.clue: Look for the action the business was not forced to take.

b.q: Tariq owns a furniture company in Brisbane. Which decision shows CSR instead of only meeting his legal duties?
opts: He pays timber suppliers a fair price above what they ask
He fits the safety equipment that workplace laws require
He pays company tax on the profit the business earns
He lowers prices to beat a rival furniture company
b.why: Paying suppliers a fair price beyond what they ask is a voluntary act that treats others fairly. Fitting required safety equipment is tempting, but it is a legal duty, so it does not go beyond the law.
b.clue: Ask whether the law would have forced the business to do it.

a.best: A bakery chooses to donate unsold bread to a local shelter

b.best: He pays timber suppliers a fair price above what they ask

problems.detail: The right option is the only one that says the bakery 'chooses' to act. This echoes the card's 'CSR is a choice', so a student could pick it from the word alone without understanding CSR.

'A fair price above what they ask' is confusing: it suggests the suppliers are asking for less than a fair price. The card also lists workers, communities and the environment, not suppliers, so students must stretch the definition. Wording such as 'pays timber suppliers fairly and buys only from sustainably managed forests' would tie the option more clearly to the card.

proposal.remember: CSR goes past legal duties and past profit to help people and the planet.
